p.src: Now the king, having seen that Sun Wukong possessed the holy art of summoning dragons, stamped their travel document with the royal seal and was about to return it to the Tang Monk and let him continue westward. The three Daoists were so alarmed that they fell to their knees in the Golden Throne Hall and submitted a plea. The emperor immediately descended from the dragon throne and hurried to raise them with his own hands, saying, “Why do my state preceptors perform such a profound obeisance today?” The Daoists said, “Your Majesty, we came here to uphold the realm, protect the country, and bring peace to its people. After twenty years of hardship, this monk has now used his magic to seize the credit and cast us aside, ruining our reputation. If Your Majesty pardons a capital offense merely for the sake of one rainfall, would that not make too light of us? We beg Your Majesty to withhold his travel document for now and let us brothers contest with him once more. What do you say?” The king was thoroughly muddleheaded, turning east when told east and west when told west. He actually took back the document and asked, “State Preceptor, how will you contest with him?” Great Immortal Tiger Strength replied, “I shall challenge him to seated meditation.” The king said, “State Preceptor, you are mistaken. That monk comes from the Chan Buddhist tradition. Surely he first mastered the mysteries of meditation before daring to obey the imperial command to seek the scriptures. How can you challenge him in this?” The Great Immortal said, “My form of seated meditation differs from the ordinary kind. It has a special name: ‘Manifesting Holiness upon the Cloud Ladder.’” The king asked, “What is ‘Manifesting Holiness upon the Cloud Ladder’?” The Great Immortal replied, “We require one hundred tables, fifty for each meditation platform, stacked one atop another. Neither contestant may climb up with his hands or mount by ladder or stool. Each must ride a cloud to the platform, sit down, and remain motionless for an agreed number of hours.”

p.src: Seeing that this posed some difficulty, the king issued an order asking, “Monk, my state preceptor wishes to challenge you to seated meditation by ‘Manifesting Holiness upon the Cloud Ladder.’ Which of you can do it?” Wukong heard this and pondered in silence. Bajie asked, “Brother, why don’t you say anything?” Wukong said, “Brother, to tell you the truth, whether it be kicking heaven, toying with wells, churning seas, overturning rivers, carrying mountains, chasing the moon, shifting the Dipper, or moving the stars, I can perform every such feat; even if it means having my head chopped off, my brains split, my belly cut open, my heart gouged out, or undergoing some extraordinary transformation, I am not afraid; but if it comes to seated meditation, I am beaten. How could I ever have the temperament to sit still? Even if you chained me to an iron pillar, I would still clamber up and down. You could never expect me to sit still.” Tripitaka suddenly spoke up: “I can meditate.” Wukong said joyfully, “Excellent, excellent! How long can you remain seated?” Tripitaka replied, “When I was young, I met eminent Chan monks who taught me the Way. By fixing my nature and preserving my spirit at the very root of life itself, I could sit for two or three years, even at the pass between life and death.” Wukong said, “Master, if you sit for two or three years, we may as well abandon our quest for the scriptures. At most it will be only two or three hours before you come down.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, the trouble is that I cannot get up there.” Wukong replied, “Go forward and accept the challenge. I will take you up.”

p.src: The elder accordingly pressed his palms together before his chest and said, “This poor monk can meditate.” The king ordered the decree proclaimed and the meditation platforms erected. A whole nation has strength enough to overturn mountains; in less than half an hour, two platforms had been set up on either side of the Golden Throne Hall.

p.src: Great Immortal Tiger Strength descended from the hall and stood at the center of the steps. With one bound he stepped onto a mat-sized cloud, went straight up to the western platform, and sat down. Wukong plucked out a hair and transformed it into a false likeness of himself, which stood below beside Bajie and Sandy; he himself became a five-colored auspicious cloud, lifted the Tang Monk into the air, and carried him straight to the eastern platform, where he sat down; then he withdrew the auspicious radiance, changed into a tiny cicada, and flew to Bajie’s ear, saying, “Brother, keep a close watch on Master, and don’t go talking to my double.” The idiot laughed and said, “I understand, I understand.”

p.src: Now Great Immortal Deer Strength had sat upon an embroidered stool watching for a long while. When neither of the two men on the high platforms had gained the advantage, the Daoist decided to lend his elder brother a hand: he plucked a short hair from the back of his head, rolled it into a little ball, and flicked it upward. It flew straight to the Tang Monk’s head, changed into a huge bedbug, and bit the elder. At first the elder felt an itch, and then he felt pain. The rule of the meditation contest was that one must not move one’s hands; whoever did so lost. Presently the pain became unbearable. He hunched his head down and rubbed the itch against the front of his robe. Bajie said, “This is bad! Master’s having an epileptic fit.” Sandy said, “No, it is a bout of headache.” Hearing them, Wukong said, “My master is a sincere and honorable gentleman. If he says he can meditate, he most certainly can; if he says he cannot do something, then he simply cannot. How could a gentleman speak falsely? You two be quiet and let me go up to take a look.”

p.src: Good Wukong gave a buzz and flew onto the Tang Monk’s head. There he saw a bedbug the size of a bean biting his master. He hastily pinched it off, then scratched and rubbed the spot for him. No longer in pain or itching, the elder sat upright upon the platform. Wukong thought to himself, “A monk’s head is so bare that not even a louse can settle on it. How could there be such a bedbug? One of those Daoists must have played a trick to harm my master. Ha! This contest will be pointless if neither side wins. Let old Monkey go and play a trick on him!” Wukong flew up and alighted on an ornamental beast’s head atop the Golden Hall. Shaking himself, he changed into a centipede seven inches long, went straight to the hollow of the Daoist’s nose, and stung him. The Daoist could no longer sit steady. He tumbled head over heels from the platform and nearly lost his life, but fortunately the many officials, high and low, caught and rescued him. The king was greatly alarmed and immediately ordered the grand preceptor in attendance to take him to the Hall of Literary Brilliance to wash and compose himself. Wukong again mounted an auspicious cloud and carried his master down before the steps. The elder had won.

p.src: The king now ordered that they be allowed to depart. Great Immortal Deer Strength submitted another plea: “Your Majesty, my elder brother has long suffered from a hidden disorder of wind. When he climbed to that great height, he was exposed to the wind of heaven, which caused his old illness to recur and thus allowed the monk to win. Keep him here a little longer and let me challenge him to guess an object through a partition.” The king asked, “What do you mean by ‘guessing an object through a partition’?” Deer Strength replied, “This poor Daoist has the art of knowing objects hidden behind a partition. Let us see whether that monk is capable of the same. If he guesses better than I do, let him depart; but if he fails, let Your Majesty determine his charge and sentence. Thus may the grievance of us brothers be avenged, and the favor earned by our twenty years of protecting the kingdom remain unsullied.” The king truly was utterly muddleheaded. Following this slanderous counsel, he immediately issued an order for the palace attendants to carry a vermilion-lacquered cabinet into the palace hall. He instructed the queen to place a treasure inside it. Presently it was carried out and placed before the white jade steps. The king told the monk and the Daoist, “You two parties are competing in magic. Guess what treasure is inside that cabinet.”

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Disciple, how can we learn what is inside the cabinet?” Wukong drew in his auspicious radiance, changed back into a tiny insect, and alighted on the Tang Monk’s head. “Master, don’t worry. I’ll go and take a look.” The Great Sage flew softly onto the cabinet, crawled beneath one of its legs, and found a narrow crack between the boards. He squeezed inside and saw a red-lacquered tray holding a set of court robes: a Jacket of Mountains, Rivers, and the Realm, and a Skirt of Heaven, Earth, and All Lands. He picked them up and shook them into disarray, then bit the tip of his tongue and sprayed a mouthful of blood over them with a sharp hiss, crying, “Change!” At once they became a filthy, tattered old robe. Before leaving, he also pissed on it. Then he crawled back out through the crack, flew to the Tang Monk’s ear, and said, “Master, just guess that it is a filthy, tattered old robe.” Tripitaka said, “He told us to guess a treasure. How can a filthy old rag be any sort of treasure?” Wukong said, “Never mind that. You need only guess correctly.”

p.src: The Tang Monk stepped forward and was about to make his guess when the Immortal Deer Strength said, “I shall guess first. Inside the cabinet are a Jacket of Mountains, Rivers, and the Realm, and a Skirt of Heaven, Earth, and All Lands.” The Tang Monk said, “No, no. Inside the cabinet is a filthy, tattered old robe.” The king said, “This monk is insolent! He dares mock our kingdom as possessing no treasures, guessing some filthy old rag.” He ordered, “Seize him!” The two ranks of officers were about to lay hands on him. In alarm, the Tang Monk pressed his palms together and cried, “Your Majesty, please spare this poor monk for the moment and let the cabinet be opened first. If it truly is a treasure, I shall accept my punishment; but if it is not, would this poor monk not have been wronged?” The king ordered them to open it and see. The attendant officers opened it at once and brought out the red-lacquered tray. Sure enough, upon it lay a filthy, tattered old robe. The king flew into a rage and said, “Who put this thing in there?” The three palace consorts emerged from behind the dragon throne, and the empress said, “My lord, I placed the Jacket of Mountains, Rivers, and the Realm and the Skirt of Heaven, Earth, and All Lands there with my own hands. I do not know how they turned into this thing.” The king said, “My queen, please withdraw. I understand. Everything used in the palace is made of satin, silk, damask, or gauze. How could there be any such filthy rag?” He ordered, “Carry the cabinet up here. We shall personally hide another treasure in it and test them again.” The emperor then went into the inner palace, plucked from a tree in the imperial garden an immortal peach as large as a bowl, placed it inside the cabinet, and had the cabinet carried down for them to guess again.

It is an immortal peach.” Tripitaka guessed, “It is not a peach, but a bare peach stone.” The king shouted, “We placed the immortal peach there ourself. How could it be a stone? Some spirit or deity must be secretly helping him.” Hearing this, Bajie gave Sha Monk a faint, knowing sneer and said, “He still doesn’t know that our brother is an old hand at eating peaches.”

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Here we go again!” Monkey said, “Let me go and have another look.” With a buzz, he flew off again, slipped inside, and saw that it was a young boy. The Great Sage was indeed resourceful: few under heaven could match his transformations, and such quick-wittedness was rare in all the world. He shook himself, changed into the likeness of an old Daoist priest, entered the cabinet, and called, “Disciple.” The boy asked, “Master, where did you come from?” Monkey said, “I came by the art of escape.” The boy asked, “What instruction have you come to give me?” Monkey said, “That monk saw you enter the cabinet. If he guesses that you are a Daoist acolyte, won’t we lose again? I have come especially to consult with you: shave your head, and let us have them guess that you are a monk.” The boy said, “Do with me as you please, Master, so long as we defeat him. If we lose to him again, not only will our reputation suffer, but I fear the court will cease to respect us.” Monkey said, “Well spoken. Come here, my boy. If we beat him, I shall reward you handsomely.” He changed his golden-hooped staff into a razor, clasped the boy in his arms, and said, “Good lad, bear the pain and make no sound while I shave your head.” In a moment the hair was shaved off; he rolled it into a ball and stuffed it into a cranny at the foot of the cabinet. Putting away the razor, he stroked the boy’s bald head and said, “My boy, your head now looks like a monk’s, but your clothes do not match. Take them off, and I shall transform them for you.” The Daoist boy was wearing a pale-green crane cloak of cloud-patterned figured silk with embroidered brocade edging, and he obediently took it off. Monkey breathed a breath of immortal air upon it and cried, “Change!” At once it became an ocher-colored monk’s robe, which he put on the boy. Then he plucked two more hairs, changed them into a wooden fish, handed it to the boy, and said, “Disciple, listen carefully: if they call for a Daoist acolyte, you must on no account come out. But if they call for a monk, push open the cabinet lid, strike the wooden fish, recite a Buddhist scripture, and climb out. Only then will our plan succeed.” The boy said, “I can recite the Scripture of the Three Officials, the Scripture of the Northern Dipper, and the Scripture for Dispelling Calamities, but I cannot recite Buddhist scriptures.” Monkey asked, “Can you invoke the Buddha’s name?” The boy replied, “Amitabha Buddha! Who cannot say that?” Monkey said, “Very well, very well. Just invoke the Buddha’s name, and save me the trouble of teaching you. Remember it well. I am off.” He changed back into a tiny insect, slipped outside, flew to Tang Sanzang’s ear, and said, “Master, just guess that it is a monk.” Tripitaka said, “This time he is certain to win.” Monkey asked, “How can you be sure?” Tripitaka said, “The scriptures declare, ‘The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are the Three Treasures.’ A monk is therefore also a treasure.”

Come here, my boy. If we beat him, I shall reward you handsomely.”
He changed his golden-hooped staff into a razor, clasped the boy in his arms, and said, “Good lad, bear the pain and make no sound while I shave your head.”
In a moment the hair was shaved off; he rolled it into a ball and stuffed it into a cranny at the foot of the cabinet.
Putting away the razor, he stroked the boy’s bald head and said, “My boy, your head now looks like a monk’s, but your clothes do not match.
Take them off, and I shall transform them for you.”
The Daoist boy was wearing a pale-green crane cloak of cloud-patterned figured silk with embroidered brocade edging, and he obediently took it off.
Monkey breathed a breath of immortal air upon it and cried, “Change!”
At once it became an ocher-colored monk’s robe, which he put on the boy.
Then he plucked two more hairs, changed them into a wooden fish, handed it to the boy, and said, “Disciple, listen carefully: if they call for a Daoist acolyte, you must on no account come out.
But if they call for a monk, push open the cabinet lid, strike the wooden fish, recite a Buddhist scripture, and climb out. Only then will our plan succeed.”
The boy said, “I can recite the Scripture of the Three Officials, the Scripture of the Northern Dipper, and the Scripture for Dispelling Calamities, but I cannot recite Buddhist scriptures.”
Monkey asked, “Can you invoke the Buddha’s name?”
The boy replied, “Amitabha Buddha! Who cannot say that?”
Monkey said, “Very well, very well. Just invoke the Buddha’s name, and save me the trouble of teaching you.
Remember it well. I am off.”
He changed back into a tiny insect, slipped outside, flew to Tang Sanzang’s ear, and said, “Master, just guess that it is a monk.”
Tripitaka said, “This time he is certain to win.”
Monkey asked, “How can you be sure?”
Tripitaka said, “The scriptures declare, ‘The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are the Three Treasures.’
A monk is therefore also a treasure.”

p.src: While they were speaking, the Great Immortal Tiger Strength said, “Your Majesty, the third object is a Daoist acolyte.” They called and called, but the boy refused to come out. Tripitaka joined his palms and said, “It is a monk.” Pigsy shouted at the top of his voice, “There is a monk inside the cabinet!” The boy suddenly pushed open the cabinet lid and climbed out, striking the wooden fish and chanting the Buddha’s name. The civil and military officials on both sides were so delighted that they cheered in unison. The three Daoists were so frightened that they stood speechless.

p.src: The king said, “This monk must have ghosts and spirits assisting him. How could a Daoist enter the cabinet and turn into a monk? Even if a court barber followed him inside, he could only have shaved his head. How could his clothes fit so well, and how could he also know how to invoke the Buddha’s name? State Preceptor, let him go.” The Great Immortal Tiger Strength said, “Your Majesty, we have met our match: this is a contest between worthy opponents. I shall put to the test the martial arts I learned in my youth on Mount Zhongnan and wager with him to the end.” The king asked, “What arts do you possess?” Tiger Strength said, “All three of us brothers possess certain magic powers: we can have our heads cut off and put them back on again; we can have our bellies slit open and our hearts cut out, yet grow whole once more; and we can bathe in a cauldron of boiling oil.” Greatly alarmed, the king said, “All three are paths to certain death.” Tiger Strength said, “We possess such powers, and that is why we dare speak so boldly. We are resolved to wager with him before we desist.” The king called out, “Monk from the Eastern Land, my state preceptor refuses to release you. He still wishes to wager with you on beheading, disembowelment, and bathing in boiling oil.”

p.src: Monkey stepped forward and said, “Your Majesty, this humble monk knows how to be beheaded.” The king asked, “How can you know how to be beheaded?” Monkey said, “When I was cultivating myself in a monastery years ago, I once met a visiting Chan monk who taught me a method of beheading. I do not know whether it is any good, so today I shall try it out.” The king laughed and said, “That young monk knows nothing of the world. How can beheading be something to try out? The head is the foremost of the six yang organs; once it is cut off, death follows at once.” Tiger Strength said, “Your Majesty, that is precisely what we want of him, so that we may vent our anger.” The foolish ruler believed his words and immediately issued an edict ordering an execution ground to be prepared.

p.src: As soon as the edict was proclaimed, three thousand imperial guards formed ranks outside the palace gate. The king ordered, “Let the monk be beheaded first.” Monkey cheerfully replied, “I shall go first! I shall go first!” With hands respectfully clasped, he called aloud, “State Preceptor, forgive my presumption in going first.” He turned his head and strode outside. Tang Sanzang seized him and said, “Disciple, take care! That is no place for games.” Monkey said, “Why should I fear them? Let go of me and wait for my return.”

p.src: The Great Sage went straight into the execution ground, where the executioners seized him, bound him tightly, and forced him onto the raised earthen mound. Then came the cry: “Strike!” With a swish, his head was struck off. An executioner then kicked it away, and it rolled like a watermelon for some thirty or forty paces. Not a drop of blood came from the Pilgrim’s neck. A cry came from his belly: “Head, come back!” Alarmed by such powers, the Immortal Deer Strength immediately recited an incantation and ordered the local earth gods and deities: “Hold his head fast. Once I have defeated this monk and reported my victory to the king, I shall enlarge your little shrines into great temples and replace your clay images with properly gilded statues.” As it happened, those earth gods and deities obeyed him because he commanded the magic of the Five Thunderbolts, and they truly held the Pilgrim’s head down in secret. The Pilgrim called again: “Head, come back!” But the head seemed rooted to the ground and would not move at all. Growing anxious, the Pilgrim clenched his fists and gave a mighty heave, snapping every rope that bound him. Then he shouted: “Grow!” With a rush, a new head grew from his neck. Every executioner was terrified, and every man of the imperial guard trembled with fear. The supervising officer hurried back to court and reported: “Your Majesty, after the little monk’s head was cut off, another one grew in its place.” Bajie said with a cold laugh, “Brother Sha, who knew our elder brother had such a trick?” Sha Monk replied, “He has seventy-two transformations, so naturally he has seventy-two heads.”

p.src: Before they had finished speaking, the Pilgrim came over and called, “Master!” Tripitaka was delighted. “Disciple, was it hard on you?” he asked. “Not at all,” said the Pilgrim. “It was rather good fun.” Bajie asked, “Elder brother, do you need medicine for the sword wound?” The Pilgrim replied, “Feel it and see whether there is any scar.” The fool reached out and felt his neck, then grinned foolishly and cried, “Marvelous! Marvelous! It has grown back perfectly—not the slightest scar where it was severed.”

p.src: While the brothers were still rejoicing, they heard the king order that their travel document be brought out. “I pardon you of all wrongdoing. Go quickly, go quickly.” The Pilgrim said, “Though we may take the document, the National Preceptor must also go to the execution ground and have his head cut off. He too should try this novelty.” The king said, “Great National Preceptor, that monk will not let you go either. Since you wagered against him, you must go—but do not frighten me.” Tiger Strength had no choice but to go. Several executioners bound him and threw him to the ground; with a flash they cut off his head, kicked it away, and sent it rolling more than thirty paces. No blood came from his neck either, and he too cried, “Head, come back!” The Pilgrim promptly plucked out a hair, breathed magic breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It changed into a yellow dog, which raced into the ground, seized the Daoist’s head in its jaws, ran straight to the Imperial Waters River, and dropped it there. Of this no more need be said.

Pitiful indeed: though he possessed the arts of summoning wind and rain, how could he compare with a true immortal who had attained longevity? In a moment he toppled into the dust. When the onlookers examined him, they found a headless yellow-furred tiger.

He fell dead in the dust and proved to be a headless yellow-furred tiger.” On hearing this report, the king turned pale with shock and stared fixedly at the two Daoists. Deer Strength rose and said, “My elder brother’s allotted life and fortune have come to an end, but how could he possibly be a yellow tiger? That wretched monk has used a deceptive transformation to turn my elder brother into a beast. I shall certainly not spare him now. I insist on wagering with him that we shall cut open our bellies and tear out our hearts.”

p.src: Hearing this, the king finally recovered his composure. Again he called, “Little monk, the Second National Preceptor still wishes to wager against you.” The Pilgrim said, “This little monk has long abstained from cooked food. While coming from the west the other day, I happened upon a charitable household that pressed a meal on me, and I ate several steamed buns too many. My belly has ached these past few days; perhaps worms have grown inside it. I was just hoping to borrow Your Majesty’s knife, cut open my belly, take out my entrails, and wash my spleen and stomach clean, so that I may properly journey west to see the Buddha.” On hearing this, the king ordered, “Take him to the execution ground.” The crowd moved in, some supporting him and others pulling him along. The Pilgrim shook off their hands and said, “There is no need to support me. I can walk there myself. Only one thing: you must not bind my hands, for I shall need them to wash my entrails.” The king issued an order: “Do not bind his hands.”

p.src: Swaying jauntily from side to side, the Pilgrim went straight to the execution ground. He leaned against the great stake, undid his sash, and bared his belly. An executioner looped one rope around his shoulders and neck and bound his legs with another. He flourished a short ox-ear knife, sliced across the belly, and stabbed an opening into it. The Pilgrim pulled his belly open with both hands, took out his intestines and organs, and spent a good while sorting them strand by strand. Then he put them back inside, coiled just as they had been before. Pinching the edges of his belly together, he breathed magic breath upon them and cried, “Heal!” At once it grew together as before.

Take your document and go.” The Pilgrim laughed. “The document is a small matter. It was you who chose to oppose him, so please go, please go.” Deer Strength replied, “Set your mind at ease. I certainly shall not lose to him.”

p.src: Just look at him: imitating the Great Sage Sun, he swaggered straight into the execution ground. The executioners looped the ropes around him, then with a ripping stroke of the ox-ear knife cut open his belly. He too took out his liver and intestines and began arranging them with his hands. The Pilgrim immediately plucked out a hair, breathed magic breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It instantly changed into a hungry eagle, which spread its wings and talons, swooped down, and snatched away all his vital organs, heart, and liver. No one knew where it flew to feast upon them. The Daoist was left a dripping specter with an empty body and torn belly, a wandering ghost bereft of organs and intestines. The executioners kicked down the great stake and dragged the corpse over to inspect it. Ah! It proved to be a white-furred, antlered deer.

His true form was a white-furred, antlered deer.” The king said fearfully, “How could he be an antlered deer?” The Immortal Antelope Strength then memorialized, “Since my elder brother is dead, how could he have revealed the form of a beast? That monk has used sorcery to frame and murder us all. Let me avenge my elder brothers.” The king asked, “What powers have you with which to defeat him?” Antelope Strength replied, “I shall wager with him that we bathe in a cauldron of boiling oil.” The king ordered a great cauldron to be fetched and filled with fragrant oil, and told the two of them to proceed with their wager. The Pilgrim said, “Many thanks for your gracious consideration. This little monk has not bathed for a long time, and my skin has been dry and itchy these past two days. I may as well go and have a good soak.”

p.src: The officer in charge duly set down the cauldron of oil, piled dry firewood beneath it, kindled a fierce blaze, and brought the oil to a rolling boil; then he ordered the monk to enter first. Pilgrim pressed his palms together and said, “Am I to bathe in the civil manner or the martial manner?” The king asked, “What is the civil manner? And what is the martial manner?” Pilgrim replied, “In the civil manner, one does not remove one’s clothes. One folds one’s arms like this, goes down and rolls over once, then comes straight back out, without soiling or damaging one’s garments. A single spot of grease counts as defeat. For the martial manner, one must bring a clothes rack and a towel, strip off one’s garments, and leap in; then one may turn somersaults and stand on one’s head at will, bathing as though it were sport.” The king said to Immortal Ram-Power, “Will you compete with him in the civil manner or the martial manner?” Immortal Ram-Power replied, “If we use the civil manner, I fear his clothes may have been treated with some drug that keeps out the oil. Let us use the martial manner.”

Tossing waves and churning the oil, he played about as though bathing in water. Seeing this, Eight Rules bit his finger and said to Sha Monk, “We have misjudged that monkey. Usually we taunt and jeer at him just to provoke him for sport. Who knew he truly possessed such abilities?” The two of them muttered together, praising him without end.

The executioner took an iron skimmer and dredged through the cauldron. But the skimmer’s mesh was wide, and Pilgrim had transformed himself into so tiny a nail that, however it swept back and forth, he slipped through the holes. How could they ever scoop him out? They reported again, “The monk was slight of body and tender of bone; he has been fried away entirely.” The king ordered, “Take the other three monks down for execution.” The guards on either side thought Eight Rules looked the fiercest, so they seized him first, threw him down, and bound his arms behind his back.

p.src: In alarm, Tripitaka cried aloud, “Your Majesty, grant this poor monk a brief reprieve. That disciple of mine has performed deed after meritorious deed since entering our faith. Today he offended the Imperial Preceptor and died in the oil cauldron, but as the saying goes, those who die before us become spirits. How would this poor monk dare cling to life? Indeed, just as all officials under Heaven govern the people under Heaven, if Your Majesty commands your subject to die, how could your subject dare refuse? I ask only that Your Majesty extend your mercy and grant me half a bowl of cool rice gruel and three sheets of paper offerings. Allow me to go before the oil cauldron and burn a string’s worth of spirit money, thereby expressing the bond between master and disciple. After that I shall submit to punishment.” Hearing this, the king said, “Quite so. Those people from the Central Realm are often deeply loyal.” He ordered that some gruel, rice, and yellow spirit money be brought for him. They duly fetched them and handed them to the Tang Monk.

p.src: Hearing this, Eight Rules said, “Master, that is not how you should pray. Sha Monk, pour out the gruel and rice for me, and let me deliver the prayer.” Lying bound on the ground, the idiot puffed angrily and cried, “You disaster-making damned monkey, you witless Protector of the Horses! You deserved to die, damned monkey; you were boiled in oil, Protector of the Horses. The monkey’s account is settled, and the Horse-Keeper’s line is ended.” At the bottom of the oil cauldron, Sun Pilgrim heard the idiot cursing wildly. Unable to endure it, he resumed his true form and stood at the bottom of the cauldron, dripping wet, as he shouted, “You swill-guzzling oaf! Who are you cursing?” When the Tang Monk saw him, he cried, “Disciple, you frightened me to death!” Sha Monk said, “Elder Brother is truly an old hand at feigning death.”

p.src: The civil and military officials were so alarmed that both ranks rushed forward and reported, “Your Majesty, that monk was not dead! He has climbed out of the oil cauldron again.” Fearing that he would be accused of deceiving the court, the supervising executioner reported again, “He did die, but the date was inauspicious, so the young monk has returned as a ghost.” Pilgrim flew into a rage at these words. He leapt from the cauldron, wiped off the grease, put on his clothes, drew out his cudgel, dragged the supervising executioner over, and struck him once on the head, reducing him to a lump of flesh. “What ghost am I supposed to be?” he demanded. Terrified, the officials hurriedly untied Eight Rules, knelt on the ground, and pleaded, “Forgive us! Forgive us!” The king descended from the Dragon Throne and tried to leave, but Pilgrim went up into the hall and seized him. “Your Majesty, do not run away. Let your three Imperial Preceptors take their turns in the oil cauldron.” Trembling all over, the emperor said, “Third Imperial Preceptor, save our life! Enter the cauldron quickly, and do not let the monk strike us.”

p.src: Immortal Ram-Power descended from the hall, removed his clothes just as Pilgrim had done, and leapt into the oil cauldron, where he too contrived to bathe in the same fashion. Pilgrim released the king, went over to the oil cauldron, and told the fire tenders to add more wood. Then he reached out and tested it. Ah! The supposedly boiling oil was ice-cold. He thought to himself, “When I bathed, it was scalding hot, yet when he bathes, it is cold. I understand now. Some Dragon King or other must be protecting him here.” He sprang at once into the air, uttered the spell of the syllable “Om,” and summoned the Dragon King of the Northern Sea. “You horned earthworm, you scaly loach! Why are you helping this Daoist? Why have you placed a cold dragon beneath the cauldron so that he can display his holiness and defeat me?” The Dragon King was so frightened that he repeatedly bowed assent and said, “Ao Shun would never dare assist him. The Great Sage does not know the whole matter. That evil creature underwent a period of bitter cultivation and managed to shed his original shell, but only his Five Thunder Method was authentically transmitted. All his other arts were picked up from heterodox schools, so he can scarcely attain the Way of the Immortals. This is the ‘Great Flaying’ art he learned at Little Mount Mao. The other two had their spells broken by the Great Sage and revealed their true forms. This one likewise refined the cold dragon himself. It is fit only for deceiving ordinary people as a trick; how could it deceive the Great Sage? This little dragon will now take away his cold dragon, and I guarantee that his bones will shatter and his skin will scorch.” Pilgrim said, “Take it away at once and spare yourself a beating.” The Dragon King transformed into a whirlwind, swept down beside the oil cauldron, seized the cold dragon, and carried it away to the sea. Of this no more need be said.
